newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: French sailor well, search for Briton continues.
newsitem.headline: French sailor well, search for Briton continues.

text.p: Australian rescue authorities said on Tuesday they were unlikely to know for two days if British solo round-the-world yachtsman Tony Bullimore was alive, trapped in the hull of his upturned yacht in the Southern Ocean.
Hopes for 56-year-old Bullimore's safety were raised when authorities noticed a change in the signal from a manually-operated distress beacon believed to be aboard his yacht.

A search plane meanwhile dropped a VHF radio to a second yachtsman, French sailor Thierry Dubois, 29, who was safe aboard a life raft dropped to him on Monday when he was found clinging to the hull of his capsized craft.

"He's indicated he is exceptionally well...he doesn't believe he has any injuries," said Australian Defence Force spokesman Colonel Andrew Reynolds, who described the Frenchman as "very happy and laughing".

The two competitors in the Vendee round-the-world yacht race sent out distress calls late on Sunday after sailing into fierce winds and giant seas in the Southern Ocean about 1,400 nautical miles (2,600 km) southwest of Perth.
A Royal Australian Navy frigate HMAS Adelaide was steaming to the area from Perth but was not expected to arrive for another two days, said Australian Maritime Safety Authority spokesman David Gray.
The frigate would pick up Dubois and try to discover if Bullimore was aboard his yacht, either by cutting a hole in the bottom of the hull or sending a diver underneath.

A change in Bullimore's distress beacon signal, which was switched to alert mode overnight, boosted hopes that he might still be alive. "That can only be activated by a person or by a freak wave moving something around in the cabin," Gray said.
However, officials said the yachtsman would battle to survive under the hull of the boat for another two days without food and water, and with a possibly diminishing air supply.
"We will continue to search the area to make sure there is not another liferaft out there, and that is our hope," said Reynolds.
Wind conditions had eased to 25 knots from 45-50 knots earlier in the rescue but the yachtsmen continued to face a five metre swell in freezing seas.

The rescue, the most distant attempted by Australian authorities, is taking place about 120 nautical miles south of the region where another competitor in the Vendee Globe race was saved from his sinking yacht 11 days ago.
Australia's Defence Industry Minister Bronwyn Bishop said on Tuesday the rescue of Frenchman Raphael Dinelli had cost about A$154,000 (US$122,000).

However, in spite of some criticism of the cost of such operations, she said money spent saving yachtsmen was not wasted: "We save lives because they're worth saving and because we have an obligation to do so."
